title: Three hundred years of the Khalsa
word: Three hundred years of the Khals
hook: crowds gather at Anandpur Sahib to mark three hundred years of the Khalsa
tomorrow: Four hundred years of the Granth

segments.voice: Yesterday, writing the history, and your line was write it down. Did a family story make it onto paper? Today, a week ends, and the path starts counting anniversaries. Day one thousand twenty-two.

A town in the Shivalik hills, its roads packed with people on foot, on tractors, on the backs of trucks. Saffron and blue everywhere. Langar tents stretching along the roadside, serving anyone who sits down. Nagar kirtan processions singing their way toward the gurdwara. The place is Anandpur Sahib, and the crowds have come home to the spot where, tradition says, the Khalsa was born on a Vaisakhi morning. The count has reached a round number. Today: three hundred years of the Khalsa.
screen: `ROADS PACKED WITH PILGRIMS.` → `ANANDPUR SAHIB.` → `A ROUND NUMBER.`

segments.voice: First, the morning being remembered. In the tradition Macauliffe records, Guru Gobind Singh stood before the gathered Sikhs at Anandpur at Vaisakhi and asked for a head. One by one, five came forward. They became the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, and they received amrit. Then the Guru asked them to give amrit to him. The teacher asked his own students to initiate him. This path told that story long ago. Today it's being remembered. Second, the gathering. When the count reached three hundred years, Sikhs came back to Anandpur Sahib in crowds, and gurdwaras far from Punjab marked it with kirtan, amrit ceremonies and nagar kirtans in their own streets. Third, what an anniversary does. It counts back to a beginning and asks: are we still the people that morning made? Fourth, this week's answer. Look back at the last seven days. Volunteers tore down a rebuilt shrine and raised it again with their own hands. A sangat cleaned a pool by passing basins along a line. A soft-spoken Sikh led India's government. A Partition orphan became the flying Sikh. A physicist sent light around a bend. Writers kept the story, in many languages. That's the panth's long line, still running from that morning: ordinary Sikhs, keeping faith in public, three centuries on. That's today's line: three hundred years.
screen: `FIVE CAME FORWARD.` · `BACK TO ANANDPUR SAHIB.` · `ARE WE STILL THAT PEOPLE?` · `THIS WEEK'S ANSWER.` · then, large: `THREE HUNDRED YEARS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for a beginning. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one beginning in your own life that still matters: a wedding, a birth, a move, a first day, a promise you made. Breathe in, and go back to that morning: where you were, who was there. Breathe out, and ask the anniversary question gently: am I still the person that morning made? Let the answer be honest, and let it be kind. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

Three hundred years of the Khalsa. The anniversary of the Vaisakhi at Anandpur, when, tradition says, the Panj Pyare stepped forward, marked with crowds at Anandpur Sahib and in gurdwaras far from it. Today's word.
screen: `THREE HUNDRED YEARS OF THE KHALSA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: three hundred years. Today, celebrate one anniversary: your own, a friend's, or your community's. Send a message, light a candle, or tell the story of how it began. Day one thousand twenty-two.

you give him amrit, as he asks.
